·
第4️⃣ 天：从满洲里往呼伦湖解锁美丽的风车秋色，在呼伦湖荡秋千欣赏静谧的湖水，沿途前行抵达186彩带河，登高俯瞰蜿蜒曲折的额尔古纳河，傍晚抵达黑山头，赴一场草原绝美日落，晚餐吃当地特色的烧烤
·
第5️⃣天：从黑山头前往恩和俄式的童话乡村，彩色木刻楞小屋搭配秋日田园，满满的异域田园风情，午后打卡整片金黄白桦林秋风落叶氛围感拉满，一路游玩抵达额尔古纳休息，领队带我们去吃了牛排锅地道好吃
·

第7️⃣天：自由行简单逛逛，吃地道的内蒙火锅，然后返程

Published Oct 8, 2026, 5:53 AM EDT

Paul Farrelly is a Contributing Writer for Screen Rant’s Gaming section and the founder of GeekGasm.org, a site dedicated to celebrating all things gaming, from triple A blockbusters to weird and wonderful indie hits. Based in Louth, Ireland, Paul has spent years writing about games, pop culture, and tech, turning his lifelong love of gaming into a career that lets him talk (probably too much) about what makes this industry so endlessly fascinating.
He’s previously written and collaborated with several entertainment outlets, including LADbible, gaining a wide perspective on how gaming fits into today’s pop culture conversation. His work blends genuine enthusiasm with thoughtful analysis, exploring how design, storytelling, and community have made gaming one of the most creative mediums around.
When he’s not glued to a controller or keyboard, Paul’s usually spinning vinyl, plotting his next horror marathon, or debating which Resident Evil entry really reigns supreme.

The Crunchyroll Anime Future Forum took place on October 7, 2026. The idea behind the forum is to bring industry leaders together along with creators and innovators to deliver future news about the platform to a wide audience. For those who aren't in the know, Crunchyroll is a massively successful anime streaming service that has been around since June 2006. This year's event led to an announcement that just might reshape the relationship of Crunchyroll with gamers. A new era is about to begin!

Sony's CEO and President of Entertainment, Hideaki Nishino, made the announcement during this year's Crunchyroll Anime Future Forum that Crunchyroll was being integrated into the PlayStation platform in brand-new ways. Crunchyroll will be getting its very own dedicated hub on PlayStation consoles in Spring 2027. Rather than falling under the usual media tab on the home bar, it's expected that Crunchyroll will have its very own section and be integrated on the home screen unlike before.

Sony acquired Crunchyroll in 2021 through Sony Pictures and since then, many cross-platform collaborations have been implemented. Having a dedicated hub on the PlayStation 5 is completely new though, and some fear it might feel like aggressive advertising for non-subscribers who just want to play their library of games. Having to scroll past an advert for Solo Leveling just to get to the upcoming Uncharted 5 icon on the home screen seems like an annoyance to many. However, how deep the integration goes hasn't been confirmed yet.

Quote from Hideaki Nishino at the Crunchyroll Anime Future Forum 2026:

"Whether longtime anime fans or discovering a series through a game, character or world they already love, players will have a dedicated place to discover anime and anime-inspired games and easily access the full Crunchyroll app."

Little is known about the upcoming dedicated hub except that it is hoping to bring together anime and anime-inspired gaming all under one umbrella. With both gaming fan bases and anime fan bases often intersecting, it seems wise to have a small niche carved out on the PS5 home screen for people to search for all things anime all in the one space. With PS Productions currently working on a game-inspired anime series, Ghost of Tsushima: Legends, it seems fitting that cross-overs in gaming and anime should be visible under a dedicated hub.

This is a pretty nice bit of news for PlayStation fans that should come as a small respite from the deluge of bad news from the company over the last few months. Between PlayStation's stance on physical discs to price increases, it's not been the best year for them. A bit of anime is a welcome distraction.

The Crunchyroll app is currently available on the PS5 with some content available to watch for free and new users can sign up for a 7-day free trial. There are also multiple paid tiers available to enjoy the full catalog of anime content ad-free. With the lines between anime and gaming blurring, its likely we'll see plenty more cross-overs, campaigns and integrations for years to come. A Chainsaw Man game made by Shift Up (the team behind Stellar Blade) would be absolutely amazing! Or perhaps an Attack on Titan/Elden Ring crossover somewhere down the line. The potential for cross-overs is endless.

items.title: PC Gamer magazine's new issue is on sale now: World of Warcraft: Forever
items.author: robert.jones@futurenet.com (Robert Jones)
items.summary: This month, PC Gamer delivers world-exclusive access to World of Warcraft: Forever, the exciting new evolution of classic WoW that is kicking off a new MMO
items.text:
This month, PC Gamer delivers world-exclusive access to World of Warcraft: Forever, the exciting new evolution of classic WoW that is kicking off a new MMO golden age. Not only do we play Forever extensively, but PC Gamer also speaks directly to many of the key devs at Blizzard who have made it a reality. And, we're pleased to say that, finally, the old WoW magic is back!

Issue 428 UK / 416 USPC Gamer magazine: $4.99
Cover story: World of Warcraft: Forever

This month, PC Gamer delivers world-exclusive access to World of Warcraft: Forever. Plus, Total War: Warhammer 40,000 previewed, The Blood of Dawnwalker reviewed, and PC gaming fans tested.

Buy this issue in print: $4.99 (US) | $16.49 (UK)

Buy this issue digitally: $4.99 (US) | $16.49 (UK)

This issue also boasts one of the fattest preview sections of the year, with PC Gamer going hands-on with a wide variety of hot incoming games, including Total War: Warhammer 40,000, Rainbow Six Tactics, Stronghold 4, 1666: Amsterdam, Lego Skylines, Afterworld, Sanctuary: Shattered Sun, and Bodycam.

(Image credit: Future)Meanwhile, the PC Gamer reviews machine passes judgement on The Blood of Dawnwalker, Metal Gear Solid IV: Guns of the Patriots, Star Wars Zero Company, Fields of Mistria, Onimusha: Way of the Sword, and Sovereign Tower, among others.

(Image credit: Future)All that plus a group test on top PC case fans, a reinstall of legendary neo noir action game, Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne, the commencement of a brand new diary where we play as a corporate serial killer in Starfield, a look at an ambitious new mod for Stardew Valley that lets you play it in 3D and VR, a developer-led deepdive into the conception of Forbidden Solitaire, a love letter to playing games with gyro aim, a fresh dispatch from The Spy, an editorial face off fight debating whether PC gaming belongs in the living room, an authoritative review of the Ryzen 7 7700X3D processor, a special report on GTA 6's glitzy Netflix reveal, and much more, too. Enjoy the issue!

Cover feature: World of Warcraft: Forever

(Image credit: Future)Written by: Heather Newman

Magazine exclusive: Until October 26th, 2026

What's in this month's cover story: PC Gamer not only gets exclusive hands-on access to Blizzard's stunning reboot of classic WoW, but also speaks to numerous of its key developers about the epic journey they have been on to bring it to life. And, yes, we're calling it already: a new golden age of MMOs is about to begin. The old World of Warcraft magic is back!

Additional content in this month's issue

LEAD PREVIEW

Total War: Warhammer 40,000

Our lead preview of this issue sees PC Gamer go hands-on with what we're already considering the most epic Warhammer 40K RTS of all time. Total War: Warhammer 40,000 is simply massive in scale and spectacle, with website editor Fraser Brown very much living the grimdark dream while playing it. Find out why in this awesome 6-page preview.

LEAD REVIEW

The Blood of Dawnwalker

Meanwhile, our lead review this issue sees us go fangs-on with Rebel Wolves' dark fantasy RPG, The Blood of Dawnwalker. An exquisite tone and strong action make this a great debut for the studio, although our reviewer finds the game's interesting approach to the passage of time not fully committed to. Our official verdict awaits.

MOD SPOTLIGHT

Stardew 3DVR

There's already been loads of great mods released for Stardew Valley, but none that have delivered quite such a dramatic shift in perspective as Stardew 3DVR, an ambitious new mod that lets you play the game in 3D and, if you have a VR headset, in VR, too. We install the mod to see just what it offers today.

REINSTALL

May Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne

Remedy's classic neo-noir action game has gone down in PC gaming history as a classic, but as magazine editor Rob finds after reinstalling the game this issue, maybe not for all the reasons it should've. From the game's engaging slow-mo action, through its pitch-perfect noir tone, and onto its deep, philosophical writing, Max Payne 2 continues to age like a fine wine.

DIARY

Starfield

An out-of-this-world new diary kicks off this issue as we attempt to play as a corpo serial killer in Starfield. Can we maintain a facade of corporate competence while also bumping off innocents with wild abandon? Or will it all end in a swift, brutal bloodfest? We pick up our axe (which whispers sweet nothings to us) to find out.

SPECIAL REPORT

GTA 6

This month's special report delves into GTA 6's dramatic reveal, covering everything from the unofficial leaks through to the glamorous Netflix gameplay first look. Can PC gamers expect a launch on PC sooner than expected? And is there good news on the game's predicted PC system specs?

GROUP TEST

PC fans

Keeping your PC cool is a key part of maintaining optimal in-game performance, so this month we test out six of the best new PC fans on the market today. And, with options ranging from budget-friendly to premium, we find recommendations for every PC gamer.

...and more!

Now Playing: The PC Gamer team writes about their adventures in Star Wars Zero Company, How to Fish, Iron Nest, and Cat Mail Co.

They're Back: Matthew Elliott re-reviews Dredge, TMNT: Shredder's Revenge, and The Tide Isle Hotel.

Making of: Rick Lane speaks to the developers behind this year's indie smash hit, Forbidden Solitaire, to discover how the game was conceived and then delivered.

items.title: Muramasa: Revenant Blades has 108 swords, and its definitive update for PC wants to make sure you use them all
items.author: wesley@pcgamer.com (Wes Fenlon)

items.text:
The Japanese Sword Museum in Tokyo, set along the bank of the Sumida river, enshrines behind glass a collection of remarkable blades spanning hundreds of years of craftsmanship. Books about the longer uchigatana and shorter wakizashi, some of them written by the museum's very donors, celebrate the swordsmiths who hammered them out of steel. But flip through one, and there's a good chance you won't spot the name Muramasa, despite his swords playing a prominent role in some of Japan's most famous battles.

(Image credit: Future)Centuries of mythology building up around the idea that your swords were cursed will tend to do that to a guy.

Vanillaware's Muramasa: Revenant Blades, at least, isn't afraid to lean into the legacy. The 2D action game is so in love with swords it's got 108 of them, and it turns the superstition that Muramasa's swords had to taste blood once unsheathed into a simple but enticing mechanic: Each comes with a unique skill, which can be equipped on another sword only after it's had its fill of bloodshed.

"There's definitely this reputation that the swords of Muramasa are cursed, but what that means is they have power," says director Wataru Nakanishi. "In this game Muramasa is an important character and will create these very powerful swords, but in turn [the protagonists] must collect souls for him, so they have this cooperative relationship based around this dark situation."

In a way Revenant Blades is lifting a curse of its own: 17 years after the game was first released on the Nintendo Wii as Muramasa: The Demon Blade, it's somehow the first release from Vanillaware to make it to PC. The Japanese studio followed Muramasa with more nuanced games, like 2019's acclaimed 13 Sentinels: Aegis Rim and 2024 tactics RPG Unicorn Overlord, but after playing Muramasa on PC I can see why the studio started here. I remember a hack-and-slash with art so lavish seeming novel back in 2009, and somehow that's just as true today.

Hey, that wave looks awfully familiarVanillawareLook at all those abilities…VanillawareEven basic ronin are a threat if you don't aggressively break their guardVanillawareThere's our guy: Muramasa himselfVanillawareRevenant Blades is rebalanced to make more of its 108 swords relevantVanillawareCool horse.VanillawareThe painterly art has a timeless quality to it, though that's something of an illusion. "It was a lot of work, and it was very difficult," Nakanishi said, laughing. "We had some of the assets, but not others. For those we had to pull them from the game, and then artists individually by hand had to touch them up and recreate them to make something appropriate for the HD release. But you know, through that arduous hand-drawn process, we were able to create this warm and colorful art that we think people will be happy to see."

Revenant Blades is also not the simplistic game I remember. The skill system for all 108 blades is new, allowing me to equip three ground and three air abilities to a trio of blades I could have equipped (and swap between) at any one time. That made for a dizzying number of special moves to keep in mind, though executing them is as simple as tapping a button and a direction.

On the harder difficulty enemies now come streaming onto the screen in daunting numbers, and with more health to compensate for your improved arsenal. I learned the hard way not to play too defensively: Blocking a few attacks would wear down my sword until it snapped, leaving me open to a quick death. Survival demands fluid strings of combos, flitting between swords to keep them from breaking, chaining a launcher skill into a rapid series of slashes that can pummel a whole gang of ninja at once.

Somehow frogs are scarier than ninjas (Image credit: Vanillaware)Or toads. I walked underneath a waterfall, not realizing I was underleveled for that bit of Muramasa's freely explorable map, and got absolutely embarrassed by a family of poison-spitting toads. Way scarier than the guys with shurikens and bombs.

In the original game enemies scaled with you as you leveled up, but Vanillaware scrapped that for Revenant Blades. Enemies in different areas now have fixed levels; you'll be able to steamroll the ones that are weaker than you, but depending on the path you take you might run into fights that send you scampering away unless you're really good.

Because you could previously only use a single skill that was locked to the single katana you had in-hand at any given moment, Nakanishi says players naturally gravitated to the most powerful late-game blades. "It kind of limited the scope of the gameplay," he says, but now that you can equip skills independently, "players have access to so many more skills and playstyles."

"Using the skills Celestial Slash and Flame Barrage, you can knock people into the air with fire, then jump up and use the aerial skill to knock them back to the ground. That kind of combination wasn't really something you could do with the more limited skill system."

In addition to possessed princess Momohime who I played as for the hour-long demo, Revenant Blades piles on a range of playable characters first added in a 2013 Vita re-release, each with their own stories. It's now a deceptively beefy game, and the skill system feels like the key it needed to unlock its full potential. I can't imagine a better fit for the Steam Deck OLED, where its vivid backgrounds will threaten to tear the eyes away from the action for the three seconds it'll take to wind up dead.

If Muramasa: Revenant Blades is the hit on PC it deserves to be, perhaps it will manage to dispel the myth that PC ports are as taboo in the halls of Vanillaware as the swordsmith's weapons have become over the centuries. Could more follow in its wake?

"We currently don't have any specific plans of that nature, but we would love to see Muramasa be successful enough that people start to ask about that kind of thing," Nakanishi says.

items.text:
Nivalis Nights is overwhelming. Intentionally, I suspect, to give me the immersive experience of living in a hyper-capitalist megacity hellscape. It has no map because Nivalis is canonically unmappable, only a HUD compass where my 20+ active quest markers all scuttle over each other, nearly as crowded as the alleyways of its layered, neon city where hundreds of citizens amble between giant apartments and fusion food joints.

(Image credit: ION Lands)Need to know

What is it?: A quest-heavy cyberpunk shop simulation in a city obsessed with debt.
Release date: September 29, 2026
Expect to pay: $25 / £22
Developer: Ion Lands
Publisher: 505 Games
Reviewed on: Intel Core Ultra 7 265, RTX 5070 Ti, 32GB RAM
Multiplayer: No
Steam Deck: Unspecified
Link: Steam

One of those joints is mine. Ramen Noir is a floundering noodle bar left to me by a friend named Thaddeus who flees the city for mysterious reasons, saddling me with its complementary insurmountable debt of 50,000 Lims.

Thaddeus also left me a greenhouse. A salty lad named Crabface bequeaths me a boat. Some lady named Ma Gomba wants me to grow her enoki mushrooms. Danny Danetti wants my opinion on his donut recipes. A sentient vacuum needs my help fleeing the human wife of his deceased former consciousness. CorpSec Agent Teleshko suggests, nay, demands that I expand my operation by buying additional businesses. Oh, right, and there's a serial killer at large who's taking out people with massive amounts of debt. You know, like me.

That's at least 21 quest markers on my HUD. (Image credit: Ion Lands)Folks, I am just trying to scrape out a profit serving chicken noodle soup and beer while I hoof it back and forth from the market buying nearly-expired ingredients on the cheap until I can afford to hire a general manager who will free me up to pursue even one of these quests.

My day in Nivalis looks like this:

8:00: Fast travel to the Docks district and sprint down the ramshackle catwalks to my greenhouse to pick the onions and potatoes I grew in my farming modules overnight.

8:30: Fast travel to Meridian Market to put my produce in the fridge at Ramen Noir for the day before my general manager starts a restock order.

8:30 - 11:30: Assist my staff for the breakfast rush by using the food processor station eight times and grabbing a couple plates of food to deliver to customers bellied up to the bar, choosing to "make polite small talk" with new customers and "offer 10% discount" to some returning ones.

11:30: Spot my not-really-rival and donut seller Danny Danetti hanging near my kitchen waiting to ask my opinion about a recipe.

(Image credit: Ion Lands)

11:30 - 12:00: Visit the greengrocer and drinks vendor in the Central Canyon district to buy and drop off all the ingredients on my shopping list for my new sake bar which doesn't have a GM yet.

12:00: Meet up with my landlord Pilk Dane who wants to accuse me of subletting (read: having any guests at all).

13:00: Receive a mysterious communication from an unknown employer demanding I go visit the crime scene of the latest serial killing and have a conversation with my automata digital assistant Ava about whether to comply or not.

14:00: Somehow become involved in seeking out the memories CorpSec erased from the past of a large guy calling himself the Miso Baron.

14:00 - 17:00: Spend too long fussing with the kitchen layout at the sake bar by putting the sink for dishwashing near the kitchen access door and the drink machine station perpendicular to the bar.

(Image credit: Ion Lands)

17:00: Use the photo mode to take a nice aesthetic shot of my remodel in the evening neon glow.

18:00: Fiddle with my staff schedule at Ramen Noir, increasing my waiter's happiness by shortening her shift and compensating by docking the pay for my robot Waiter X5 by 0.50 Lims, sorry.

18:00 - 21:00: Help serve cocktails at Sake Bar to turn a bit of profit faster than my staff would alone.

21:00 - 24:00: Stumble through the extremely confusing and layered Hive Mall district to find a furniture vendor, thinking I'll buy a couple extra chairs, but ultimately chickening out of spending the money.

24:00 - 1:00: Open my quest log, see that I still haven't started the ones related to using my boat and purposefully ignore them because I just really dislike fishing in games.

2:00: Stay out past curfew to filch some chairs from the restaurant next to Ramen Noir, dodging CorpSec security camera beams, so I can add them to Sake Bar to serve more customers—for profit!

(Image credit: ION Lands)Just a slice, please

Nivalis Nights calls itself a "slice-of-life" sim, which is a close enough description of what you get when you borrow life sim decorating, shop sim management, open-ish world exploration, farm sim produce production, and bungee cord them all together with a surprisingly story-heavy quest structure.

In the first five-ish hours, I worried that the genre soup of Nivalis Nights was going to ultimately disappoint me. Everything I found to praise about it came with a caveat.

Seems great

BUT

Exploration

The city is beautiful to look at and the layered, extremely vertical level design makes the possibility of exploring it seem fascinating.

There isn't much drive to explore aside from finding more silent vendors, sitting to eat similar meals at rival restaurants, and a scavenger hunt for broken fuse boxes.

Management

Shop management has some neat layers like customizing recipes with different ingredients and optimizing efficiency of kitchen layout and work shifts.

Babysitting my shops by actively participating feels a little dull with very repetitive customer appearances and awkward first-person cooking animations.

Decorating

Renovating restaurants with new cabinet styles or decorations seems like catnip for a build mode fiend like me, especially with free, non-grid placement.

Placing furniture and cabinets in first person without snapping to walls is actually really finicky and being strapped for cash means I don't really get to indulge in beautification.

Romance

Completing quests with certain characters can also lead to pursuing romances with them.

The payoff on the couple I've tried is a date with a shortish conversation and no further acknowledgement of being in a relationship.

(Image credit: ION Lands)

It's a personality hire

What I found after several hours and a couple in-game weeks in Nivalis is that the characters are the star feature. I'll allow myself a heavy-handed food metaphor, given the context: The characters and setting are the eggs of Nivalis Nights. Whip 'em up with those dry ingredients and they become a leavening agent to make that batter rise, baby.

The streets of every district are jam packed with people. Many are unnamed, silent NPCs but a surprising number are fully voice-acted characters with stories and quests, some of whom can eventually work at my shops. Sometimes they don't seem immediately relevant until suddenly I'm five steps deep into someone else's quest and they ask me to find a specific hacker who, oh wait, I know that guy!

Their stories run a full neon spectrum from comedic corporate satire to strikingly earnest stories of people crushed beneath inherited debt:

Danny Danetti sells donuts in Meridian Market district near Ramen Noir and affably undermines the CorpSec demand that businesses always compete and never fraternize by checking up on me and trading recipe ideas.

Lois Gyo is a burnt out game designer for a major corp who initially comes off as a goofy shut-in but over time really grew on me as she strives to stay positive and develop friendships in a soul-crushing environment.

Pilk Dane is my piece-of-crap landlord, a bumbling dork just trying to make a buck off people below him despite having zero intimidation factor. Finding out his side hustle made me laugh, just not in the way he intended.

Sal Magundi II is a chef with augmented arms that are presently detached from his body and working in the kitchen while he's off walking around town bellowing orders to his cooks between talking to me.

Lochlainn McKenna has the face of a corpster but he's just the gentle dad to four kids he can barely afford, including the one with a respiratory condition exacerbated by living on the lower city levels and only treatable by prohibitively expensive equipment. I don't think I'd even have seen his story if I hadn't hired him to work at my third restaurant.

There are dozens more of them (At least 121, by count of the portraits in the "known characters" section of my menu) all with nuanced stories and genuinely excellent vocal performances that really sell some of the moments when they turn from goofy caricature to gut-spillingly relatable.

The amount of quests and story content that weaves these characters into each others' lives and into the main plot of a debt-chasing serial killer stalking the lower districts is a delight. I'd expected for the shop management and decorating to be the real draw in Nivalis Nights, but instead it's this vibrant, enormous cast of characters who are really motivating me to beat the streets every day, navigating labyrinthine districts in search of the next thread to pull.

Nivalis Nights is an alright shop sim with some okay decorating and a nod to life sim romances, but it's an excellent place. It's a smog-filled techno hellscape full of people with "generational debt" loomed over by advertisements about transferring the consciousness of your pet dog into any body, forced to live in nearly religious adherence to capitalism. I'd eat up a novel set here. Lacking that, I'll probably develop strong feelings on head-canons about its characters and spend hours tooling for new angles in its photo mode long past rinsing the simulation game this world is hiding in.

I'll allow myself a heavy-handed food metaphor, given the context: The characters and setting are the eggs of Nivalis Nights. Whip 'em up with those dry ingredients and they become a leavening agent to make that batter rise, baby.

The streets of every district are jam packed with people. Many are unnamed, silent NPCs but a surprising number are fully voice-acted characters with stories and quests, some of whom can eventually work at my shops. Sometimes they don't seem immediately relevant until suddenly I'm five steps deep into someone else's quest and they ask me to find a specific hacker who, oh wait, I know that guy!
Their stories run a full neon spectrum from comedic corporate satire to strikingly earnest stories of people crushed beneath inherited debt:

Danny Danetti sells donuts in Meridian Market district near Ramen Noir and affably undermines the CorpSec demand that businesses always compete and never fraternize by checking up on me and trading recipe ideas.

Lois Gyo is a burnt out game designer for a major corp who initially comes off as a goofy shut-in but over time really grew on me as she strives to stay positive and develop friendships in a soul-crushing environment.

Pilk Dane is my piece-of-crap landlord, a bumbling dork just trying to make a buck off people below him despite having zero intimidation factor. Finding out his side hustle made me laugh, just not in the way he intended.

Sal Magundi II is a chef with augmented arms that are presently detached from his body and working in the kitchen while he's off walking around town bellowing orders to his cooks between talking to me.

Lochlainn McKenna has the face of a corpster but he's just the gentle dad to four kids he can barely afford, including the one with a respiratory condition exacerbated by living on the lower city levels and only treatable by prohibitively expensive equipment. I don't think I'd even have seen his story if I hadn't hired him to work at my third restaurant.

There are dozens more of them (At least 121, by count of the portraits in the "known characters" section of my menu) all with nuanced stories and genuinely excellent vocal performances that really sell some of the moments when they turn from goofy caricature to gut-spillingly relatable.

The amount of quests and story content that weaves these characters into each others' lives and into the main plot of a debt-chasing serial killer stalking the lower districts is a delight. I'd expected for the shop management and decorating to be the real draw in Nivalis Nights, but instead it's this vibrant, enormous cast of characters who are really motivating me to beat the streets every day, navigating labyrinthine districts in search of the next thread to pull.

Nivalis Nights is an alright shop sim with some okay decorating and a nod to life sim romances, but it's an excellent place. It's a smog-filled techno hellscape full of people with "generational debt" loomed over by advertisements about transferring the consciousness of your pet dog into any body, forced to live in nearly religious adherence to capitalism. I'd eat up a novel set here. Lacking that, I'll probably develop strong feelings on head-canons about its characters and spend hours tooling for new angles in its photo mode long past rinsing the simulation game this world is hiding in.

Netflix’s Epic New Western Rides Past 6 Million Views in Opening Week

Image via. Netflix

Netflix's grand new limited series adaptation of John Steinbeck's "East of Eden" lived up to the hype, taking the number-one spot on the streamer's latest viewership report. The show stars Florence Pugh, Christopher Abbott, and Mike Faist in the lead roles, and is spearheaded by Zoe Kazan, whose grandfather, Elia Kazan, directed the landmark 1955 adaptation of Steinbeck's novel. The new East of Eden beat out holdover hits such as Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story and the second season of The Gentlemen, both of which have held top-10 spots on the global Netflix rankings for several weeks now. It remains to be seen if East of Eden can sustain interest in the long run, but it's certainly in a strong position, given the renewed interest that Westerns have seen in recent years.

This new wave has been dominated by Taylor Sheridan's Yellowstone franchise, which also includes the old-fashioned prequels 1883 and 1923. East of Eden shares several stylistic and thematic similarities with the prequel shows, and comes on the heels of Netflix's Little House on the Prairie and American Primeval. The seven-episode limited series opened to positive reviews and appears to have settled at a "Certified Fresh" 87% score on Rotten Tomatoes. The aggregator website's consensus reads, "Zoe Kazan imbues her legacy adaptation with delicious moral quandaries and sumptuous landscapes, but it's the expanded character work from Pugh and Lee that brings justice and dignity to this new canon of East of Eden."

Collider Exclusive · 8 Questions · 2 Minutes
Which Western Icon Are You Most Like?

Four icons are waiting at the end of this: the stranger who never gives his name, the gambler who would die for a friend, the lawman who never wanted the badge, and the girl nobody has ever talked out of anything.

🃏Doc Holliday(Tombstone)

01

The town is about to learn your name. What do they call you?
In a Western, what people call you is already half the character.

AThey never do find it out, so the stranger will have to do.
BA nickname I picked up at a card table and never shook off.
CMarshal, and most people say it with a bit of respect.
DMy full name, and I will correct anybody who tries to shorten it.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

What are you carrying?
Everything out here is character, right down to what is sitting on your hip.

AOne revolver I have had for years and have never once talked about.
BA pistol, a knife and a deck of cards, and the cards do most of the damage.
CA shotgun, because it tends to end arguments rather than start them.
DMy father's gun, which is far too big for me, and I am carrying it anyway.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

What are you riding?
A hero and their horse is one of the oldest relationships in cinema.

ASomething plain that nobody in town would look at twice.
BWhatever I won last night, which may not be strictly mine yet.
CA big steady horse that will not spook when things get loud.
DA pony I overpaid for and named myself, and I will hear nothing against him.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

You have got one evening in town. How does it go?
The saloon is where these films quietly tell you who somebody really is.

AOne drink at the far end of the bar with my back to the wall.
BAt the card table, holding court, up forty dollars and climbing.

DUpstairs with the ledger, working out exactly what tomorrow is going to cost.

05

A stranger offers you money for a job that sounds like trouble.
Somebody always turns up with a full purse and a bad idea.

AI ask how much, and then I ask for a good deal more than that.
BI say yes before he has finished, mostly because it sounds like a story.
CI ask him who gets hurt if I turn him down.
DI ask for the terms in writing before anybody shakes on anything.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

Somebody is waiting for you in the street. What does the town see?
Two people, an empty road, and everybody else watching from behind the shutters.

ASomebody walking out very slowly who has not said a single word.
BSomebody grinning, which everyone watching finds deeply unnerving.
CSomebody making one last attempt to talk the other man down.
DSomebody far too young to be out there, walking out regardless.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

AExplain myself to somebody who has not earned an explanation.
BRide off and leave a friend standing out there on his own.
CLet a whole town pay for a fight it had nothing to do with.
DLet a grown man tell me I am too young to be standing here.

Eight questions in, this is the one that decides your icon.

AOn a ridge somewhere, riding away, without saying goodbye to anybody.
BSomewhere warm and worn out, having enjoyed very nearly all of it.
CHome, with the badge on the table and the whole thing behind me.
DOlder, changed by it, and telling this story for the rest of my life.

The Dust Has Settled
Your Western Icon Is…

Four icons and four completely different ways of walking into trouble.
This is the one you would have been out there, why it fits, and what it would have cost you.

The Dollars Trilogy · 1964–1966

The Man With No Name

You have never explained yourself and you have never needed to,
because people work out fairly quickly that you are the most capable person in the room
without you ever having to mention it.

Eastwood built the character out of everything he refused to do, stripping away the
backstory, the speeches and every bit of reassurance until only the competence was left.

You keep your own counsel, and while other people occasionally find that unnerving, you
have never felt any real need to fix it for them.

The Dollars films work because he genuinely is in it for himself right up until the
moment he is not, and he never explains that part either.

You would be gone before anybody got a chance to thank you.

Doc Holliday · Tombstone · 1993

Doc Holliday

You are the funniest person in most rooms and the most loyal
person in all of them, and you would be genuinely insulted if somebody suggested those two
things were in any tension.

Doc has no real reason to be in this fight beyond the fact that his friend is in it,
which is the only reason he has ever needed for anything.

You lead with wit, and it does a very effective job of hiding how seriously you take the
handful of people you actually care about.

Val Kilmer's performance is the most quoted in the entire genre because the jokes keep
getting sharper as the situation gets worse.

You would spend everything you had on this and still describe it as a good week.

Wyatt Earp · Tombstone · 1993

Wyatt Earp

You never wanted this job, and you took it anyway because the
alternative was standing there watching somebody less careful do it badly, which is the most
Western reason there has ever been.

Earp is the reluctant authority figure, a man who came to town specifically to be left
alone and somehow ended up answerable for all of it.

You are protective by instinct, so when something goes wrong your first thought is who
is exposed rather than who is to blame.

These films understand that keeping order costs far more than breaking it, and that the
person holding the line almost never gets thanked.

You would do the whole thing again, and you would complain about it the entire time.

Mattie Ross · True Grit · 1969 & 2010

Mattie Ross

Nobody has ever successfully talked you out of something you had
already decided was right, and a long line of grown adults has found that out the hard way.

Mattie is the most relentless character in the Western canon and she manages it through
argument, paperwork and flat refusal rather than a fast draw.

You have no patience for being managed, so you negotiate, you check the details and you
turn up exactly when you said you would.

True Grit is the rare Western where the moral centre is the youngest person on screen
and every adult around her has to catch up.

You would get what you came for, and the film is honest about what that takes out of
you.

EA's reboot of the Skate series is a free-to-play online game with mixed user reviews on Steam. Aspects of Skate are well-liked, but a common complaint is that it lacks the spirit of skate culture, exchanging grittiness for brand-name premium cosmetics and tidy-looking maps in an online-only ecosystem that prevents true DIY modding.

Enter ReSkate, a new "modding platform" created (with AI assistance) by a pair of coders who go by zee_x64 and ReGlitched. The modders have experience with other custom server projects, namely R5Reloaded, which allows free-to-play shooter Apex Legends to be modded and played privately.

In just a few days, ReSkate was downloaded from GitHub over 350,000 times. The software hooks into a particular version of Skate on Steam and allows it to be played offline, in custom servers, and with custom maps and other assets.

"Honestly didn't realize how big this was going to be," zee_x64 told PC Gamer over Discord this week. "We were just doing it for the love of the game."

We were just doing it for the love of the game.

zee_x64, ReSkate modder

The modders say they aren't trying to undermine Skate developer Full Circle or "replace the live game," and have no personal issues with Skate's microtransactions. "For me the game is free to play and they need to make money somehow to be able to keep developing the game," zee_x64 said.

To that end, ReSkate will only work with the current version of Skate and isn't being promoted as a way to get premium content for free. Mods that unlock premium cosmetics are disallowed, at least in ReSkate's official channels.

(But does not make it possible to cheat in official servers, because ReSkate doesn't interact at all with EA's servers.)

On the unofficial Skate subreddit, players are posting videos of custom cosmetics and maps—Counter-Strike maps made it in immediately, of course—and debating what ReSkate's effect on the live game will be.

Counter Skate 2 from r/Skate4

One person is excited simply to have the option to choose any shirt color for their avatar. "The fact I can just open up a modding tool app; design the material type; design the colour; and not wait for the devs to release a specific version and wait for it to release on rotation is just great," they wrote.

Others are less convinced that ReSkate is a boon, with some expressing sympathy for Skate's developers on the expectation that the platform will negatively affect the game's future. One popular comment speculates that EA could come to "see [Skate] as a failed experiment and shuffle resources elsewhere."

At the time of writing, EA has not commented publicly on ReSkate.

AI tools sped up development

Custom server projects for defunct MMOs and long-running live service games have been a thing for a long time, but they aren't typically released while a game is still in early access. A 2026 wrinkle in this particular case is that the modders say development was substantially accelerated by AI coding tools.

"We used AI to help reverse [engineer] the game as I don't see any reason not to when the tooling exists," zee_x64 said. "Without it, it probably would of taken years to do the same thing … that also doesn't mean we blindly just prompted AI until it worked, we still had to use our previous knowledge to get it actually working."

Antivirus flags complicate the install

A heads-up for potential ReSkate downloaders: Windows antivirus doesn't like it, and you may have to create an exception for the file to avoid it being quarantined, an uncomfortable step despite the modders' assurance that it is a false positive.

"Some antivirus software may flag ReSkate because it uses techniques that can resemble malware, such as DLL injection, process/memory modification, and downloading files over HTTPS," says kushWRA1TH, a mod in ReSkate's Discord server. "These are used for its game-mod functionality and do not by themselves mean ReSkate is malicious."

Even if ReSkate itself is not malicious, downloading and using it does carry a risk, as it could contain exploitable security flaws. (As can any software.)

The modders note as well that they cannot vouch for every fork of the code, referring to versions created by people other than the original modders. As an open source project, ReSkate's inner-workings are available for anyone to analyze or modify.

items.text:
It likely won’t surprise anyone that Unity’s just-announced AI vibe-coding game creator, Spark, is being met with derision at Kotaku. We’re not exactly enamored with genAI, it’s fair to say. But even the most generous response to the trailer that Unity has put out to promote this new tech would have to be partly made of curse words and poop emojis. It’s so bad, it could be used as a warning against the use of AI in games development.

Unity Spark is a “new way for people to come together to make and share games right in their browser,” explains Unity, boasting “no prior Unity or game development experience required.” But this isn’t “one-shotting,” the post insists. “Asking AI to regurgitate an already-invented game does not make you the next Hideo Kojima, any more than re-typing the first paragraph of War and Peace in your word processor makes you Tolstoy.” But you know what does make you both Kojima and Tolstoy? Asking an AI to make you a game using pre-made Unity assets instead. Boom.

And how? Well, it’s time to explore the extraordinary trailer.

Space Corridor

“You know that game you always wanted to make?” asks Theo in the video’s opening depiction of a text chat. “Of course…?” replies Mari. “Have you tried Unity Spark?”

Oh boy, this is Mari’s moment. She’s been planning this game for so long, but it’s not until now that she could possibly have the tools to create it. And what is Mari’s big vision? What will be realized by Spark’s promise to let her “direct your dream game?”

Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to Space Corridor.

And how does Mari thoughtfully craft the unique vision for the game she’s imagined making all these years? By typing six words into Spark!

A corridor shooter set in space. Way to dream big, Mari!

“These artist-created assets look perfect for your game,” replies Spark, offering “Assets for the Station K-7 holdout corridor: environment, player character, cover props,” which our floating cursor chooses to “add to project.” That results in a large, blue corridor, with a generic Mass Effect-ish soldier standing in the middle, and the title Space Corridor on screen. The walking animation is abysmal, but we’ll get past that as Theo and Mari start to brainstorm within Spark to add their unique twists to the project.

“Let’s add drones!!” says Theo, overcome with inventiveness, and dropping in a generic drone-shaped asset. But Mari is having none of it. She’s not willing to resort to something so obvious.

The drone vanishes as she suggests, “What about Aliens?” Capital-A Aliens. “Yes!!!” replies Theo, a whole other exclamation point added to his excitement. A grey-like alien appears and after clicking a play icon, staggers toward our hero. “Make it explode!!!” says the ever-jubilant Theo. Our soldier seemingly already knows how to shoot, and shoots, and the alien poofs out of existence with no explosion at all.

“Create the tools you need,” says Spark, trying to move on from this. Theo demands of it, “We need a tool to control lighting presets,” and a tool pops up offering a suite of options, from “Work Lights” (Bright for editing) to “Blackout” (Power failure) and “Shore Leave” (Warm & cozy). By this point, the space soldier dude appears to have learned how to perform a melee takedown, kicking the drone (Theo’s got the drone back!) out of the air above his head.

The trailer then touts your ability to “Direct gameplay,” quickly darting past some flowcharts and showing off screens that are filled with dozens of asset descriptions and taskbars that look an awful lot less like vibe-coding and a lot more like actual hard work, but are fortunately skipped over in seven seconds of rapid cuts.

With this all done, we’re treated to the vision of the future that is Space Corridor, a ghastly-looking third-person shooter in which a generic soldier shoots at a generic drone that doesn’t visibly react to being shot. Apparently it’s good enough, as Mari declares, “I think it’s ready,” and Theo agrees, “Yes!” So they hit the “Share” button, and oh my goodness it’s a breakout success.

It’s been added to 1,000 wishlists today alone! It’s getting money brought in on Co-Fi! (“Two friends made my favorite game of the year. Take my money again,” says the anonymous contributor.) The game, in which you shoot a drone in a corridor, is priced at $7.99 and has five stars from 214 reviews!

My favorite bit in this barrage of images of wishful thinking is a Discord screen in which Theo says,

remember when we said we don’t know how to make a game?

IT’S OUT

And Mari replies, “guys please wishlist it I’m shaking.”

Fortunately Dex is here to say, “NO WAY. buying it rn.”

The spark’s gone out

It’s just so perfect. It’s impossible to parody, given it does everything a good parody of the creatively bankrupt conceit would try. It’s literally called Space Corridor. That’s not a derisive title I’ve made up, but what it’s actually called in the video’s fake store pages. It depicts the creation of the most generic, poorly constructed, horribly animated, non-responsive, blandly designed, badly lit, literal gaming corridor you can imagine. This is the most ambitious, exciting, eye-catching idea Unity had when putting together its promotional material for the forthcoming technology.

But I’ve saved the best for last, a secret surprise for those who read to the end. YOU CAN PLAY SPACE CORRIDOR RIGHT NOW! You can play it in your browser here. It is so spectacularly terrible! It’s not even set in a corridor! You play in three small, sealed rooms, shooting at drones that embarrassingly ping into existence in front of you in “waves” while a timer counts down, and then you get thrown out of an airlock for your troubles. It’s about five minutes long, and it’s worse than you’re already thinking.

Unity Spark is listed as “coming soon,” with a waitlist button for excited future corridor designers to press. What a time to be alive.

items.title: Margaret Qualley leads the refreshingly grown-up romance Love Of Your Life
items.author: Caroline Siede
items.summary: One of the ironies of moviemaking is that a regular human life can seem too small to put onscreen. Living is the biggest thing any of us will ever do and yet
items.text:
One of the ironies of moviemaking is that a regular human life can seem too small to put onscreen. Living is the biggest thing any of us will ever do and yet it feels like a story about the ins and outs of everyday existence must be couched in some kind of premise or hook that can sell the story. To some degree, Rachel Morrison’s film Love Of Your Life has one. It’s a romance that explores what happens to fiercely independent nurse Maya (Margaret Qualley) after she meets-cute with adorably extroverted nerd Charlie (Gabriel Basso) when she’s 26 years old. Yet the heart of its story is anchored less in the rhythms of a romantic comedy or even a romantic drama than in the belief that the day-to-day realities of being a person are worthy of being immortalized.


With her gentle, small-scale sophomore feature, following the boxing drama The Fire Inside, Morrison is aiming for (if not quite hitting the highs of) the observational humanism that colors something like Celine Song’s Past Lives or Kelly Reichardt’s entire filmography. Several wrenching and dramatic things happen as Maya ages into her late 20s and early 30s, but Morrison presents them less as the beats of a classic melodrama and more as punctuation marks within a life that extends far beyond the logline you would use to sum it up. That makes Love Of Your Life hard to describe without spoiling it. It touches on topics ranging from marriage and family to grief and the impulse to escape reality. Yet the pleasure (and the tension) of watching it is the question of where Maya’s life will take her next—a path that’s predictable in its big beats but surprising in its small ones, anchored by Qualley’s luminously watchable screen presence.


The screenplay by Nyad writer Julia Cox is filled with well-observed grace notes, like Charlie’s complete non-jealousy around Maya’s best friendship with a guy she briefly dated in college (Patrick Schwarzenegger) or the way Maya mostly but perhaps not entirely connects with Charlie’s mom (a standout Catherine Keener) when he excitedly takes her home to meet his family. There’s an impromptu apartment celebration in the middle of a massive storm that feels like one of those perfect nights that could genuinely happen to a couple, not just something that could only take place in a movie. And the plot is rooted in a specific moment in time in a way that slowly but impactfully reveals itself.


Despite those highs, however, there are times the film pushes a touch too hard. The cast doesn’t always find a complete level of naturalism to their performances and the script occasionally falls back on overwritten exchanges and familiar platitudes, particularly in its second half, as Maya finds herself traveling the world and crossing paths with a handsome Londoner named Felix (Lanterns‘ Aaron Pierre). Still, the overall pacing is such that each time it feels like Love Of Your Life has settled into convention, it swerves in an unexpected direction. This isn’t a story with twists, exactly, but there are emotional shifts and reveals that arrive in ways that challenge our understanding of what the main characters have been running to and from.


In fact, Love Of Your Life both indulges and refutes the wave of Eat, Pray, Love-style travelogue romances that have been popping up everywhere. Working with DP Todd Banhazl, Morrison (herself an Oscar-nominated cinematographer) fills her screen with gorgeously dreamy montages of Portugal, London, Tokyo, and New Orleans. Yet Love Of Your Life doesn’t necessarily see the impulse to run away to find yourself as an inherently empowering one. Morrison is empathetic towards why her characters act the way they do, yet clear-eyed about the cost of their actions on the people around them. It all builds towards a climatic conversation that’s earnest without being overly sentimental.


Indeed, though romance drives the plot, Love Of Your Life is more of a character study of Maya than anything else. It’s her life that’s on display in all its moments, big and small, happy and sad. It’s a refreshingly grown-up perspective on a genre that has become increasingly overtaken by teen and young adult stories. The film’s title refers to the youthful optimism that you’ll one day find the person destined to be your great love. But, more importantly, it also refers to the idea that you need to learn to love your own life in both its tragedies and its ecstasies. After all, it’s the only one you’ve got.

Writer: Julia Cox

Starring: Margaret Qualley, Gabriel Basso, Aaron Pierre, Patrick Schwarzenegger, Catherine Keener

items.text:
As streaming libraries go, Hulu’s stable of original films is a bit less substantial than some of its competitors. Part of this is because Hulu has always been more focused on television, creating its own originals and offering next-day streaming for many network and cable series. The streamer primarily relies on licensing agreements to pad out its film library, often from its parent company Disney, but with plenty of other studios in the mix too. (For example, it is the streaming home of both 20th Century Studios and Searchlight Pictures.)


The streamer also has some surprisingly solid horror offerings available for those looking to get in the Halloween spirit, including originals like the Predator prequel, Prey, and the horror-comedy, Fresh, which sees Daisy Edgar-Jones dating a guy with cannibalistic tendencies. Hulu’s annual Huluween celebration also mixes both longtime seasonal favorites like Hocus Pocus, Scream, and Edward Scissorhands alongside newer hits such as Hereditary, Midsommar, and The Substance.


Here are more of our picks (in alphabetical order) of the Hulu original films you should watch.


This list was updated on October 7, 2026.

Fire Island


Cast: Joel Kim Booster, Bowen Yang, Conrad Ricamora, Margaret Cho, Matt Rogers


A queer retelling of Pride & Prejudice, this fizzy film reimagines Jane Austen’s classic as a gay romantic comedy set among a group of friends during a vacation on New York’s famous Fire Island. Horny, hilarious, and emotional by turns, the film includes all the necessary beats of an Austen tale (class issues, social hierarchies, snappy wit) while centering fresh queer and Asian American perspectives that make it stand out in a crowded adaptation field.


Good Luck To You, Leo Grande


Cast: Emma Thompson, Daryl McCormack, Isabella Laughland


On paper, Good Luck To You, Leo Grande sounds like it should be a cringe comedy. But that couldn’t be further from the truth. The story of a retired teacher (Thompson) who hires an attractive young sex worker (McCormack) to help her finally experience the pleasures of physical intimacy, this film is actually a warm and thoughtful ode to self-acceptance and body positivity. Most of the film takes place in a single location (a hotel room) and relies primarily on dialogue and character moments to carry its story. Thompson has rarely been better, and the film


Minding The Gap


Cast: Kiere Johnson, Zack Mulligan


Bing Liu’s Oscar-nominated documentary about coming of age on the economic fringe of the American Midwest explores the friendships of three young men growing up in Rockford, Illinois, brought together by their shared love of skateboarding. The film follows Liu as he reconnects with two former friends and uses a decade of archival footage to explore the ways skateboarding not only offered them an escape from the abuse they faced at home, but helped shape their paths into adulthood. Come for the heartfelt themes, stay for the gorgeous cinematography.


Palm Springs


Cast: Andy Samberg, Cristin Milioti, J.K. Simmons, Camila Mendes, June Squibb, Peter Gallagher, Tyler Hoechlin


An inventive, entertaining romantic comedy about a pair of wedding guests who find themselves stuck in a time loop and living the day of the ceremony over and over, Palm Springs is a delightful surprise on multiple levels. Silly and grounded by turns, it takes its Groundhog Day-esque premise and runs with it, adding interesting new layers as Sarah (Miloti) is introduced to a situation that Nyles (Samberg) has been trapped in for some time and the relationship between the two deepens through repeated loops. Samberg and Miloti have fantastic chemistry, and the script is a fabulous mix of romance and sci-fi tropes.


Plan B


Cast: Kuhoo Verma, Victoria Moroles, Michael Provost, Mason Cook, Gus Birney, Adrien Brody, Rachel Dratch


This quirky coming-of-age comedy follows Sunny (Verma), a sheltered Indian teen on a road trip to find a Plan B pill 24 hours after her first awkward sexual encounter is charming from start to finish. Alongside her rebellious best friend Lupe (Moroles), the pair journey across South Dakota, meeting a variety of strange and hilarious characters along the way. Director Natalie Morales deploys a light hand with what could be a painfully realistic premise, grounding the story in Sunny and Lupe’s charming and relatable friendship.


Predator: Killer Of Killers


Cast: Lindsay LaVanchy, Louis Ozawa, Rick Gonzalez, Michael Biehn


This R-rated animated anthology doubles down on the Predator franchise’s evolution as a kind of sci-fi-tinged historical fiction, using three 20-minute interconnected stories to further explore the idea that the ruthless alien race known as the Yautja have basically been using Earth as a training ground for their deadliest killers. Split into three segments that follow a Viking raider, a feudal Japanese ninja, and a World War II pilot all facing off against Predators as they vie for the ultimate title of “Killer Of Killers.” Despite the segments’ compressed runtimes, each mixes gruesome violence with complex narrative stakes.


Prey


Cast: Amber Midthunder, Dakota Beavers, Dane DiLiegro, Michelle Thrush, Stormee Kipp


A surprisingly creative and genuinely thrilling reinvention of the Predator franchise, this prequel set in the Great Plains in 1719 follows Naru (Midthunder), a young Comanche warrior who rejects the gender traditions of her tribe and wants to become a hunter. Her skills are put to the test when an unseen adversary endangers the tribe. Naru makes for an extremely likable and compelling protagonist, and the film takes the franchise back to its tense human vs. alien roots in a story that’s more about character choices than lore building.


Rye Lane


Cast: David Jonsson, Vivian Oparah, Simon Manyonda, Karene Peter, Malcolm Atobrah, Benjamin Sarpong-Bron


This quietly enchanting British romantic comedy centers on the unexpected relationship that blossoms between two young people who meet by chance in an art gallery while they’re both dealing with painful breakups. The pair spend a day together wandering the streets of South London, talking about their exes and lives and fall in love themselves along the way. The streaming landscape could use a lot more movies like this love letter to the neighborhoods of Peckham and Brixton, featuring sparkling dialogue and great chemistry between its leads.


Summer Of ’69


Cast: Chloe Fineman, Sam Morelos, Matt Cornett, Charlie Day, Paula Pell


An awkward high schooler (Morelos) hires an exotic dancer (Fineman) to help her seduce her longtime crush before graduation day in this raunchy, sex-positive teen comedy. The latest in a long line of films about high schoolers trying to get that stretches back to Fast Times At Ridgemont High but feels more like Superbad and Bottoms, Summer Of ‘69 mixes a decent dose of heart in with its horniness and hormones.


Summer Of Soul


Cast: Lin-Manuel Miranda, Chris Rock, Stevie Wonder, Nina Simone, Mahalia Jackson


This excellent documentary tells the story of the 1969 Harlem Cultural Festival, a six-week concert series that brought together an array of predominantly Black performers from the worlds of soul, jazz, and gospel. But although the festival took place during the same summer as Woodstock, it received much less mainstream coverage and is considerably less well known. Director Ahmir “Questlove” Thompson’s film changes that, combining contemporary interviews with glorious archival performance footage to create what feels like an overdue celebration as much as a history lesson.

items.text:
For all of you who have been wanting to upgrade your PC or build a new one this year, I truly sympathize. I, too, had some plans for my rig, but they're all on the back burner, as we're all trying to shield our wallets from the effects of the RAMpocalypse. Thanks, AI.

Nearly all components are affected by this point, but DDR5 RAM itself is through the roof. Unless you enjoy paying an extra $300-$500 for RAM compared to this time last year, it's just not a great time to build a new rig.

Against all odds, our team here at PC Gamer has been hard at work digging up some of the best Prime Day PC gaming deals for you over these past couple of days, and bar the occasional glimmer of hope here and there, it's pretty grim out there. So much so that I decided to check out the DDR4 situation instead.

And guess what, it's actually ... not terrible?

Have a look at all the best Prime Day PC gaming deals here.

Scaling back down to DDR4 is not the worst thing that can happen to a PC gamer. If you put the savings into a better GPU, you'll be far better off as long as gaming is your main goal. And anyway, capacity is king; fast DDR4 RAM is really nothing to turn your nose up at. You may not find these DDR4-powered rigs in our best gaming PC builds roundup, but they're still valid, and they still show a lot of promise.

The long and short of it is that choosing DDR4 in 2026 is a good way to build a budget-friendly gaming PC that'll still last you for years. More importantly, it can still be upgraded over time, but you'll probably have to choose Intel for substantial upgrades and savings.

The reason is simple: Intel's LGA 1700 socket still supports DDR4. For AMD, you'd have to go all the way back to the AM4 socket, with the only upgrade path being the iconic Ryzen 7 5800X3D or perhaps the Ryzen 7 5700X3D. That's all well and good, but you can get a better PC right now by sticking to Intel.

With Intel's LGA 1700 combined with DDR4 RAM, the savings are in the hundreds of dollars. Buy a cheaper CPU today and upgrade it to the 14700K or even the 14900K one day, which will still be a much more powerful chip than the Ryzen 7 5800X3D, even though the Ryzen chip certainly ranks among the best CPUs for gaming.

Saving over $55 on RAM in 2026 simply feels good. Not only is this DDR4 kit cheaper than DDR5 equivalents by default, but it's also heavily discounted. You're getting top DDR4 frequencies, tight timings, and the sweet knowledge that you've just saved hundreds of dollars. You can also splurge on 2x16 GB for more capacity.

Finding a cheap SSD in 2026 is next to impossible, and this is just about as good as it gets. Our tests show that it's not the fastest SSD in the world, but it's more than fast enough to handle whatever gaming shenanigans you're going to get up to, and it lets you leave some money in your wallet for other components instead.

Now, in a budget-friendly PC build, this AMD RX 9070 GRE GPU might feel overkill, and it is. But the whole point of saving on less impactful components is to make room for a solid GPU. The RX 9070 GRE is pretty much the only GPU with decent deals this Prime Day, so take advantage of it while you can. With that said, you can definitely scale back and go with a cheaper GPU in a build such as this.

This GPU isn't going to floor you with its performance, but being part of the RTX 50-series family, it can sort of cheat its way through gaming with DLSS. While you're getting slower GDDR6 memory, you're unlikely to feel it if you're not angling for max settings in resource-heavy games. With GPU prices as wild as they've been, this is actually the best budget graphics card around.

RTX 5050 price check: Walmart $399 | Amazon $369.99 | Newegg $399.99View Deal

Intel's Arc B580 might be a better use of your money if you're looking for more VRAM. It's not the fastest GPU in the world, but it's plenty good enough for 1080p gameplay, and the extra VRAM means it'll stay decent for longer than some of the 8GB alternatives available right now.

Arc B580 price check: Amazon $369.99 | Walmart $329.99 | Best Buy $349.99View Deal

The alternatives

Of course, there are alternatives. You can pick up an AMD Ryzen 5 5600X during Prime Day deals, which is now down to $147.99, and build a new PC around the AM4 platform with DDR4 RAM. You'll still save money, but you'll have a less impressive and promising upgrade path. There's even the humble Ryzen 5 5500, now just $87.95 with a 45% discount.

Ultimately, with either rig, you'll be locked to a specific motherboard and will need to make big moves to upgrade to a current-gen CPU.

Newegg has something fun going on now, too: You can build your own PC bundle with savings all around. Click around and see if you can't find a better deal than what I managed to dig up from the depths of the RAMpocalypse for you here.

The bottom line is that when times are tough and everything is overpriced, getting creative is the way to go. DDR4 RAM might be the key to getting you a great gaming PC, and even if it's not the top option right now, it's more than good enough when paired with the right GPU. Shop now while Prime Day deals last, because after that, the prices will get even worse.
